title: Cinema Seat Booking
summary: Schedule shows on screens and let many customers concurrently hold seats with an expiry and confirm bookings, without ever double-booking a seat.
statement:
A multiplex wants the booking core behind its box-office terminals and app. Popular shows open for sale at a fixed time and thousands of customers pick seats at the same moment, so seat allocation must stay correct under concurrent use.

**Screens and shows**
- A screen has a fixed seat layout: rows identified by letters (A, B, …) and seats numbered from 1 within each row. Every seat has a category, such as regular or premium.
- A show is a movie playing on a screen from a start time to an end time, with a price per seat category. Two shows on the same screen may not overlap; a show may start exactly when the previous one ends.

**Browsing**
Customers can list the upcoming shows of a movie, ordered by start time, and see a seat map of a show in which every seat is available, held or booked.

**Holding and booking**
- A customer picks 1 to 10 seats of one show and asks to hold them. The hold succeeds only if every requested seat is available at that moment; otherwise nothing is held and the response names the seats that were not available.
- A successful hold returns a hold id, the total price and an expiry time: 5 minutes after the hold by default (configurable).
- A customer may have at most one active hold per show.
- Confirming a hold before it expires turns it into a booking with a booking id. Payment is handled elsewhere and has succeeded by the time confirm is called.
- Once a hold's expiry time is reached, its seats are available to everyone again and the hold can no longer be confirmed. This must happen without anyone explicitly releasing the hold.
- A customer can release their own hold early, or cancel their own booking before the show starts; the seats become available again.
- Holds cannot be placed for a show that has already started.

**Concurrency**
The booking core is called from many threads at once. It must never double-hold or double-book a seat, never leave seats held after a failed hold, and never deadlock — whatever order customers list their seats in. Requests for different shows should not wait on each other.

All time-dependent behaviour (hold expiry, show start) must be testable without waiting in real time.

requirements.text: Define screens with a seat layout (rows, seats per row, category per seat) and schedule shows (movie, screen, start, end, price per category in paise). A show whose end is not after its start, or that overlaps another show on the same screen, is rejected; touching shows are allowed.
List a movie's shows that have not started yet, ordered by start time, and return a show's seat map with each seat's status (available, held or booked).

Hold 1–10 distinct, existing seats of a show for a customer, all-or-nothing. A failed hold holds nothing and names the unavailable seats. A successful hold returns a hold id, the total price (sum of category prices) and its expiry time. Holds for a started show, and a second active hold by the same customer for the same show, are rejected.

Confirm a hold before its expiry time to create a booking (booking id, seats, total price); its seats become booked. Confirming at or after the expiry time, confirming someone else’s hold, or confirming the same hold twice is rejected and creates no booking.
When a hold's expiry time is reached, its seats are shown as available and can be held by others, with no explicit release call. The hold duration defaults to 5 minutes and is configurable.
All holding, confirming, releasing, cancelling and seat-map operations are safe under concurrent use from many threads, with the guarantees given in the concurrency notes.

A customer can release their own active hold early, and cancel their own booking before the show starts; in both cases the seats become available immediately. Cancelling after the show has started, or acting on another customer’s hold or booking, is rejected.

constraints: Java 17 or later using only the standard library (java.util.concurrent is allowed); JUnit 5 may be used for tests.
Single JVM process with all state in memory; no database, external coordination service or network.
Up to 20 screens, each with at most 26 rows of 30 seats, and up to 1,000 shows.
The current time must come from a source that tests can control; times have second precision.
assumptions: There is a single cinema; there is no city or cinema search.
Customers are identified by a non-empty string id; there is no authentication.
A movie is identified by its title; no other movie metadata is needed.

examples.title: Hold, conflict, confirm
examples.scenario: Screen 1 has rows A and B with seats 1–5 each; row A is premium, row B regular. Show S1: "Inception" on Screen 1, 18:00–20:45, premium 35000 paise, regular 20000 paise; hold duration 5 minutes. At 17:00 U1 holds A1, A2. At 17:01 U2 asks to hold A2, A3. At 17:04 U1 confirms.
examples.expected: U1's hold succeeds: total 70000, expires 17:05. U2's request fails naming A2, and A3 is not held. U1's confirm creates a booking for A1 and A2 totalling 70000; the seat map shows A1 and A2 booked and A3 available.

examples.title: Expiry without a release call
examples.scenario: At 17:10 U3 holds B1, B2 and never confirms. At 17:15 U4 asks to hold B2, B3; then U3 tries to confirm.
examples.expected: U3's hold succeeds (total 40000, expires 17:15). At 17:15 it has expired, so U4's hold succeeds (B2, B3, total 40000, expires 17:20) and U3's confirm is rejected as expired. B1 shows as available.

examples.title: Contention
examples.scenario: Time frozen at 17:30. 50 threads, each for a different customer, simultaneously try to hold B5. Separately, for 1,000 rounds two threads simultaneously request [A4, A5] and [A5, A4] for two different customers; any successful hold is released before the next round.
examples.expected: Exactly one of the 50 holds of B5 succeeds; the other 49 fail naming B5. All 1,000 rounds complete (no deadlock) and in every round exactly one of the two requests succeeds.

examples.title: Scheduling around an existing show
examples.scenario: Schedule S2 on Screen 1 from 20:00 to 22:30; then from 20:45 to 23:15.
examples.expected: The first is rejected because it overlaps S1 (which ends at 20:45). The second is accepted because it starts exactly when S1 ends.

edgeCases: A hold request with a duplicated seat (A1, A1) or a seat that does not exist on the screen (C9) is rejected and holds nothing.
Requests for 0 seats or 11 seats are rejected.
Confirming exactly at the expiry instant is rejected.
A customer with an active hold on S1 asks for another hold on S1: rejected; once the first hold expires or is released, a new one is allowed.
Releasing or confirming a hold that belongs to another customer is rejected.
Cancelling a booking after the show has started is rejected.
Holding seats for a show that has already started is rejected.
outOfScope: Payment processing, refunds and cancellation fees.
Multiple cinemas, cities or search across them.
Persistence, REST APIs or any UI.
Coordination across several processes or machines.

concurrency.notes: Must be thread-safe: hold, confirm, release, cancel and seat-map reads may run concurrently from many threads. Guarantees: (1) concurrent holds that share any seat of the same show — at most one succeeds, and N concurrent holds of one free seat give exactly one success; (2) a hold fails only because a requested seat is held or booked by another successful hold or booking, and after a failed hold returns, none of its seats are held for it; (3) a seat is never booked twice, and confirm, release, cancel and expiry of the same hold resolve to exactly one outcome; (4) no deadlock or livelock regardless of seat order in requests; (5) each seat in a seat map shows a status it really had. Should: operations on different shows do not block each other.

acceptanceCriteria.text: An overlapping hold fails naming the conflicting seat and holds none of the requested seats, as in the first example.
With controlled time, a hold confirmed one second before expiry becomes a booking, while a confirm at the expiry instant is rejected and its seats are available to others.
50 threads holding the same seat concurrently produce exactly one success, and the seat map shows that seat held.
Concurrent requests listing the same seats in opposite orders always complete without deadlock, with exactly one success per round.
Racing confirm and release of the same hold leaves exactly one outcome: either a booking exists and the seats are booked, or no booking exists and the seats are available.
Overlapping shows on a screen are rejected while touching shows are accepted, and a movie’s upcoming shows are listed in start-time order.
Cancelling a booking before the show frees its seats; cancelling after the start, or another customer’s booking, is rejected.

stretchGoals.text: Suggest the best N adjacent available seats in a requested category for a show: same row, as close to the row's centre as possible.
Reject holds that would leave a single isolated empty seat between taken seats in a row.

rubricGuidance.correctness: FR-3 to FR-5 carry the weight: all-or-nothing holds, confirm only before expiry, and automatic availability at expiry. Replay the worked examples with controlled time, including a confirm exactly at the expiry instant (rejected).
rubricGuidance.modeling: Look for clear ownership of the fixed layout, per-show seat inventory, holds and bookings. Seat status for a show should have a single authority, and expiry should be a property of the hold rather than scattered timestamp checks.
rubricGuidance.principles: Seat status changes (available → held → booked, held → available) should be enforced in one place. Concurrency is central: check-then-act gaps, inconsistent acquisition order across seats, and seats left held after a failed hold are serious defects, whatever mechanism is chosen.
rubricGuidance.extensibility: Plausible changes: new seat categories and pricing rules, different hold durations, seat-suggestion rules (stretch). These should be local changes. A straightforward design that keeps per-show state isolated is ideal; generic frameworks and speculative abstraction earn no credit.
rubricGuidance.readability: Concurrency-sensitive sections should be small, obvious and commented where the reasoning is subtle; the hold and confirm flows should read top to bottom.
rubricGuidance.edge_cases: Expect explicit errors for unknown or duplicate seats, seat-count limits, actions on another customer’s hold or booking, double confirm, shows already started, and the expiry boundary instant.
rubricGuidance.tests: Beyond functional tests with controlled time, expect at least one real multi-threaded test asserting exactly one winner for a contended seat, and one showing opposite seat orders finish without deadlock.
